This is incorrect. In PostgreSQL, SERIALIZABLE isolation level is NOT implemented by row-level locks. Instead, PostgreSQL uses a mechanism called Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which was introduced in PostgreSQL 9.1. SSI works by detecting serialization anomalies (read-write conflicts) rather than by blocking reads with locks. 

In PostgreSQL, readers never block writers and writers never block readers (due to MVCC). At the SERIALIZABLE level, PostgreSQL tracks read/write dependencies and aborts one of the conflicting transactions when a serialization anomaly is detected. It does NOT place locks on rows that are read.

At lower isolation levels (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ), no locks are placed on read rows. At SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL doesn't use read locks either - it uses predicate locking (SSI) to detect conflicts and abort transactions, not to block them.

So the answer is "no" (false).
